offset-correction: Imagine a scale that now reads zero when empty. Do its smallest markings let you weigh a grain exactly?
Round a reading on paper. Has anything about the scale itself changed?
repeat-mean: Picture a scale that adds the same extra gram each time. Where does that gram go when you average three readings?
Imagine a hundred copies of exactly the same shifted reading. What is their average?
mean-uncertainty: Find the square root sign in the formula. What happens to the square root when its input grows fourfold?
Keep the spread fixed and increase only the number under the square root. What happens to the denominator?
combine-uncertainties: Imagine the instrument reads a little high today. Would both readings shift together?
Write the same extra amount next to both readings. What happens to those extras when you add the readings?
define-measurand: A cart speeds up. Would timing its whole trip give the same speed as timing just its last metre?
Two people use the same brand of timer at different parts of the trip. What should they agree to measure?
controlled-difference: How might the warmer water cool with the fan switched off?
List everything that changed between the trials. Can you tell which change caused the difference?
background-subtraction: Imagine making two fresh measurements of the background. Would you always subtract exactly the same amount?
Compare a small positive result and a small negative one. Does the background measurement become more precise when the sign changes?
sample-time-scale: Picture filming a slow thermometer many times a second. Can it show a temperature spike before it responds?
What information can the saved file contain if the sensor itself never followed the fast change?
calibration-gain: Try two positive inputs that are far apart. Can subtracting one fixed number change the gap between their readings?
Think of a line on a graph. Which changes when you slide it down, its height or its slope?
reference-uncertainty: Every comparison uses the same ruler. Which error would every repeat inherit?
Imagine identical readings against a ruler whose marks are slightly too far apart. What might you still be unsure about?
calibration-residual: Could a repeat measurement land a little above a perfectly straight calibration line?
Think of readings scattered on either side of a straight line. What pattern would several readings need to show?
calibration-hysteresis: Keep the units fixed. Compare reaching the same input from above and from below.
Picture a spring easing back after a stretch. Which part of its recent history might affect the reading?
sample-scatter: Imagine four readings. Their count has a square root of two. What happens if you divide the spread by two?
Both quantities have the same unit. Which describes individual readings and which describes their mean?
shared-bias: Picture a ruler missing its first centimetre. Would measuring the same way a hundred times change where its marks start?
Add the same offset to every number in a short list. Where does the offset appear in the mean?
resolution-uncertainty: A digital display shows just one decimal place. How many nearby values might round to the same display?
Picture two true lengths that fall between the same marks. What would the instrument show?
sensitivity-factor: Imagine standing at the bottom of a curved bowl. What happens to the height if you move a small distance either way?
Look at the shape of the graph just around its flat point. What change might a straight-line estimate miss?
correlated-inputs: Add the same small number to two readings, then subtract them. Track each copy of the extra number.
Try adding the two shifted readings on paper. What sign does each copy of the offset have in a sum?
least-squares: Find where the residual is squared. Does the slope of the fitted line change the sign of a square?
Try squaring a positive gap and an equally large negative gap before adding them.
weighted-fit: Which reading should count more, one with a tight uncertainty or one with a wide uncertainty?
Find the squared uncertainty in the denominator. What happens to that denominator when uncertainty doubles?
reduced-chi-square: Could two different curves pass near all the measured points within their uncertainties?
More points can test a curve more closely. Can one number tell you whether every other possible curve fails?
held-out-check: Changing a label leaves the same measurements in place. Which ones has the tuning process already seen?
If you changed the model after seeing these points, what fresh measurements could you use to test it?
reproducible-record: Imagine the correction rule changes later. Which numbers would you need to run the new correction?
Even a tiny change can matter in a later calculation. Where could you keep both versions?
drift-check: Imagine the reading climbs at noon and returns by evening. What would just two endpoint checks show?
A digital display can also warm up and cool down. When would you check for a change during the run?
expanded-uncertainty: Change volts to millivolts on the same measurements. Would that change the chance of covering the true value?
Think about the shape of the measurement errors. Which assumption links this multiplier to a coverage probability?
report-resolution: Try rounding a number and then multiplying it. How could a small rounding error grow in a later step?
Think about when a reader needs the final rounded value and when your next calculation still needs the extra digits.
